concept.name: LTI systems
concept.description: Systems that are linear and time-invariant.

cases.question: Why does knowing an LTI system's impulse response let you predict its output for any input?
cases.rubric: Must say the input can be written as a sum (integral) of shifted, scaled impulses, and that linearity plus time invariance make the output the same sum of shifted, scaled impulse responses. Naming convolution alone, without the reason, is not enough.
cases.expectedAnswer: Any input is a weighted sum of shifted impulses. Time invariance means each shifted impulse gives a shifted impulse response; linearity means the weighted sum of inputs gives the same weighted sum of those responses. That sum is the convolution of the input with h.
cases.answer: Every input is a superposition of delayed impulses scaled by the input's values. Because the system is time-invariant each delayed impulse produces a delayed copy of h, and because it's linear the scaled copies add up. So y is the convolution x * h.

concept.name: RC circuit step response
concept.description: Finding the voltage across a capacitor after a step input.

cases.question: A 10 kΩ resistor and a 100 µF capacitor in series are connected to a 5 V step at t = 0, capacitor initially uncharged. Give the capacitor voltage v(t).
cases.rubric: v(t) = 5(1 − e^(−t/τ)) with τ = 1 s, for t ≥ 0. Any equivalent form is right. A wrong τ or a sign error in the exponent is wrong.

concept.name: Stability
concept.description: Whether a system's output stays bounded, read from its poles.

cases.question: A continuous-time system has poles at s = −1 and s = −3. Is it stable, and why?
cases.rubric: Stable, because every pole has a negative real part (lies in the left half-plane), so every term of the natural response decays. Reasoning based on the poles being real, or on their magnitude, is wrong even with the right verdict.
cases.expectedAnswer: Stable: both poles have negative real parts, so the natural response is a sum of decaying exponentials e^(−t) and e^(−3t).
cases.answer: Stable, because both poles are real numbers, so there's no oscillation.

concept.name: Big-O notation
concept.description: Describing how an algorithm's running time grows with input size.

cases.question: What is the worst-case running time of binary search on a sorted array of n elements, in Big-O notation?
cases.rubric: O(log n). Any log base is fine. O(n log n), O(n), or describing the best case is wrong.
cases.expectedAnswer: O(log n): each comparison halves the remaining range.
cases.answer: O(1) if the middle element is the target.

concept.name: Treaty of Versailles
concept.description: The 1919 peace settlement between the Allies and Germany after World War I.

cases.question: What was the Treaty of Versailles, and roughly when was it signed?
cases.rubric: The peace treaty ending World War I between the Allies and Germany, signed in 1919. The year may be off by one if the war it ended is right.
cases.expectedAnswer: The 1919 peace treaty between the Allied powers and Germany that formally ended World War I.
cases.answer: The treaty after WWI where Germany had to accept blame and pay reparations, 1919.
